mcqs.question: What is the defining trait of the Adapter pattern?
options: It translates one interface into another that a client expects, without modifying either side
It adds new caching behavior to an existing object transparently
It restricts direct access to an object for security reasons
It splits a complex subsystem into several independently deployable services
mcqs.explanation: Adapter is pure translation between two interfaces, neither of which changes. Adding caching describes Decorator, restricting access describes Proxy, and splitting a subsystem is a service-decomposition concern, not a structural pattern covered here.

mcqs.question: Why do most mainstream object-oriented codebases default to the object adapter over the class adapter?
options: Object adapters are always faster at runtime
Class adapters cannot implement more than one method
Composition works without needing multiple inheritance, so it works in more languages and can adapt any subclass at runtime
Object adapters don't require an interface to be defined at all
mcqs.explanation: Object adapters hold a reference to the adaptee and delegate, which needs only composition — available everywhere — and can wrap any subclass passed in at runtime. Class adapters need multiple inheritance, unavailable in languages like Java. Speed and interface requirements aren't the deciding factors.

mcqs.question: Your XmlLoggerAdapter lets the legacy library's XmlSerializationError propagate unchanged out of log(). What's the actual problem with this?
options: It's slower than catching the exception
Python doesn't allow re-raising exceptions from adapters
The Logger interface becomes undocumented for other adaptees
Every caller of the Logger interface now has to handle a library-specific exception type, defeating the point of the interface boundary
mcqs.explanation: The adapter's job is to make the adaptee invisible to callers — leaking its exception type re-couples every caller to the legacy library. This isn't about performance or documentation, and there's no such restriction on re-raising in Python.

mcqs.question: A team wants one simplified method to trigger checkout across inventory, payment, and shipping subsystems. Which pattern fits, and why not the other?
options: Adapter, because it hides subsystem complexity behind one call
Facade, because it provides a new simplified entry point over multiple subsystem classes rather than translating one mismatched interface
Adapter, because payment and shipping APIs are always incompatible
Neither pattern applies to multi-subsystem coordination
mcqs.explanation: This is Facade's exact use case — one simple entry point over several existing classes. Adapter is for making one existing interface match what a client expects, not for coordinating many subsystems, so it's the wrong tool here even if the individual APIs happen to be incompatible with each other.
